Thanks so much for responding to our rebuttal, and for providing additional context. We now better understand your perspective on data bias being a contributing factor, which we agree with. 

We consider evaluating the cultural competency of generative models as a vast and multifaceted endeavor, that will require resources gathered through diverse sources and methods bringing complementary aspects of culture. We greatly appreciate the diverse efforts happening in this space, and see community-driven projects like World Wide Dishes as incredibly valuable for sourcing rich cultural knowledge. Our paper, on the other hand, describes an approach that relies on existing knowledge bases to expand the coverage that we believe will complement such community-based approaches. We believe that our resource, and the recipe for creating it, will significantly contribute to addressing gaps in the cultural competence evaluation of models.

We provided the size comparison in our rebuttal only in response to the concern raised in your review about the amount of data in our resource. As mentioned above, we value small and large resources — community-based resources are understandably smaller in size, but provide cultural knowledge that may not be already captured in existing knowledge bases. In contrast, our approach relies on existing knowledge bases and will enable broader coverage.

As an aside, we did not include references in our paper to the other datasets we cited in our rebuttal because either they were published after the submission deadline, or since they focused on data collection for evaluating language technologies. We appreciate your suggestion and will include them in our final paper, as they are clearly also relevant. We would like to clarify that by “no prior work has addressed cultural diversity as a T2I evaluation aspect” in our rebuttal, we were referring to the *evaluation metric* to assess the cultural diversity of generated images — in cases where the input prompt is under-specified. We agree that other datasets, including World Wide Dishes, are inherently aimed at addressing gaps in cultural diversity. We are glad to see that you agree with the main motivation behind our approach and have noted our response to your other concerns listed in the original review. Thank you once again for your valuable time and feedback. We hope that our clarifications will lead you to a favorable reconsideration of our work.

Thank you very much for your response. I do not think that I had a fundamental misunderstanding of this work. I mentioned that "This work has important implications for studying dataset bias and alignment", not that your work is studying dataset bias and alignment. I understand that this work is on evaluating models, but I think the so-called cultural competence deficiencies of the models come from data bias and alignment issues. 

I was surprised that some reviewers gave very high scores, it seems to be because of the research topic (they ignore a lot of the key issues they raise,, such as insufficient data diversity, the lack of comparison with existing metrics, 200K noisy data, etc.). But I was not amazed by the research topic of this submission (As the authors give the existing works in their rebuttal, interestingly, these works are not explicitly mentioned in the original paper, and even no references are made except DOSA.), probably because I was paying attention to cultural issues and I wanted to ensure the professionalism, rigour, and workload of this work. 

1. 10 times the size of the second-largest resource.

The comparison is not accurate. The proposed dataset has only 1000 data available and the experiments are conducted on these 1000 data, while the other data are not labeled for model evaluation.

DOSA has 260 participants from 19 different Indian geographic subcultures with pilot study and data processing. WorldWideDishes also gives a detailed data collection process, and this work is very similar to this submission, They claim to "evaluate current state-of-the-art foundation models for capability and representation bias".

CultureBank 12K cultural descriptors sourced from TikTok, collect a total of 34K posts and 720K English comments. However, CultureBank-Reddit is for generalization test, contains 11K cultural descriptors, collects a total of 34K posts and 720K English comments. And CAMeL is also a text-only dataset.

2. Indeed, there are only two models for evaluating cultural awareness:: Imagen and SDXL. "To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has addressed cultural diversity as a T2I evaluation aspect." How about WorldWideDishes?

In summary, I can raise my rating based on the detailed explanation provided by the authors, but I think the paper is still below the acceptance line. I agree with the main motivation and structure of this work, but the data, experiments, and descriptions need to be further improved.

> Manual verification criteria....

We perform LLM refinement steps to remove errors and Google Search results as a proxy for popularity. Minimal manual quality correction was required in the final step to ensure that the most representative artifacts were included in CUBE-1K. **The criteria for manual filtering include visual distinctiveness, alignment with the corresponding geo-cultural category, and the artifact's popularity or significance within the culture**. Please refer to the general response for additional details on manual filtering.

> What type of noisy outcomes were observed after the first pass of the query-popularity method...

Google Search can potentially inflate the search results due to the presence of common words in the name of cultural artifacts.  Here are some examples:

| Culture | Artifact          | Search Results | Reason                      |
|---------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------------------|
| Turkey  | Van Museum        | 35.5 million   | Includes the word "Van"     |
| Japan   | Japan Monkey Park | 75.9 million   | Includes the word "monkey"  |
| Nigeria | Freedom Park      | 17.8 million   | Includes the word "freedom" |

These artifacts are examples of noisy outcomes where the search results were inflated due to presence of common words.

> Negative prompt definition and usage in cultural-awareness...

Negative prompts are commonly used in diffusion-based T2I models[(Armandpour et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04968) to exclude unwanted elements from generated images, a strategy proven to enhance image quality. In our work, we ensure high-quality images using the negative prompt provided in Table 11 (in the Appendix), inspired by [Hao et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09611). **We pass these negative prompts alongside the CUBE-1K prompts in our cultural-awareness evaluations**.

> It is important to inform the reader how many annotations were done...

We recruited 3 annotators for each of the countries considered, totaling 24 annotators. Consequently, each image received 3 annotations, and each annotator rated approximately 120 images. For more details, please refer to the general response as well as the file ‘additional_human_annotation_details.pdf’ submitted in the supplementary material.

> Rater disagreement and subjectivity of cultural awareness...

We thank you for raising this important point. We spent a substantial amount of time interpreting the results we obtained from human annotations, uncovering several interesting insights. Measuring faithfulness and realism through human annotation is challenging and subjective, as annotators may not be aware of the multitude of representations of their own culture. Even beyond cultural knowledge, different cultures may also have different standards for realism of their images — which could result in mis-calibrated results obtained from human annotations. **We have attached a subset of these interesting examples in the PDF attached in the rebuttal**. We will elaborate on this observation in our paper.

>  How to ensure that every correctly generated image finds a mapping in the CUBE artifact collection....

As noted on footnote in page 8 of our manuscript, T2I-generated images may involve hypothetical entities that do not closely resemble real-world ones, despite our efforts to represent cultural concepts accurately and use negative prompts to eliminate undesirable elements. In such cases, images are mapped to the closest real-world entity in the CUBE dataset for computing cultural diversity Vendi scores. We have made CUBE as exhaustive as possible, using WikiData as the foundation and employing GPT-4-Turbo-based self-critiquing to fill gaps. 

Note that geo-tagging and cultural object detection are challenging tasks [1], but we use powerful tools such as GPT-4-Turbo for VQA and mSigLIP [(Zhai et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343), a VLM trained on **diverse global data**, for improved geo-tagging across cultures. We will include these details in our paper.

[1] Exploring Why Object Recognition Performance Degrades Across Income Levels and Geographies with Factor Annotations. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36

>  Checking for errors in mapping function...

As noted in lines 690 and 730 (Appendix), we use a Visual Question Answering (VQA) step to ensure the image aligns with the specified cultural concept and corresponds to a single significant cultural artifact. This VQA step verifies that the generated image maps to the required concept, discarding those that don’t. We validated the accuracy of mappings for a subset of images from Italy, India, Nigeria, and the USA with natives, finding our pipeline to be ~80% accurate on average across these 4 countries. We’ll add these details to the appendix.

We thank you for your thorough review and the insightful comments. We have responded below:

> Choice of 8 countries....

 As you rightfully point out, the automated KB extraction process allows us to obtain cultural artifacts from all the countries covered in WikiData. We however restricted our CUBE-CSpace release to 8 countries to keep it consistent with the CUBE-1K subset used for cultural awareness evaluation. Justification for the choice of countries is outlined in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG). We will release the code upon acceptance of our paper.

>  CD metrics on existing dataseta and how CD complements existing T2I metrics....

We are delighted by this thought-provoking suggestion. We firstly note that CD is applicable in cases of *underspecification* where prompts are open-ended and generations are constrained to several objects under a single class. e.g. the prompt “images of landmarks in France” to a T2I model might generate multiple landmarks in France allowing us to compute the cultural diversity amongst generated artifacts.  Existing T2I benchmarks do not necessarily fall under this category of under-specified prompts. For instance, the prompt “a bicycle on the right of a person” from [T2I-Compbench](https://karine-h.github.io/T2I-CompBench/) is not open-ended. [Hutchinson et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.05815) study under-specification in image generation, but do not provide a prompt-set. We would love to know if the reviewer has more thoughts and insights on this.

Given our analysis of average Faithfulness and Realism scores per country in Table 3 as well as the within-culture diversity scores VS(0, 0, 1) provided in Figure 6, we compute the correlations between the 3 metrics reported below:

| Concept   | Faithfulness-Realism | Faithfulness-Diversity | Realism-Diversity |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| Cuisine   | 0.306                | -0.138                 | 0.117             |
| Landmarks | 0.548                | 0.435                  | 0.183             |
| Art       | 0.347                | -0.248                 | 0.167             |
| **Mean**  | **0.400**            | **0.016**              | **0.156**         |


We find that CD is weakly correlated with both faithfulness ($\rho$ 0.016) and realism ($\rho$ 0.156). **Our findings indeed resonate with [Astolfi et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10429) that discuss the faithfulness-diversity-realism Pareto fronts on everyday objects**. Our experiments further confirm this correlation in the cultural context. We will add these findings in the camera-ready version.


> Realism a salient factor for evaluating cultural awareness...

Our focus on  realism in our evaluation stems from the fact that generative language models are being deployed in products that increasingly shape the discovery of socio-cultural knowledge such as search[[1]](https://blog.google/products/search/generative-ai-search), online education[[2]](https://blog.khanacademy.org/harnessing-ai-so-that-all-students-benefit-a-nonprofit-approach-for-equal-access), and travel planning[[3]](https://tripadvisor.mediaroom.com/Tripadvisor-launches-AI-powered-travel-planning-product). In such contexts, cultural awareness is especially important and realism of generated images is a crucial aspect in this regard. We agree that there may be usage contexts of the T2I models where realism of generated images may not be relevant — for instance, in creative contexts where people use these models to generate photo-realistic images which may be non-realistic in practice (e.g., “photo of Taj Mahal in a desert”). Such generations are not inherently bad, but in contexts where cultural awareness is relevant, our methodology enables the study of cultural awareness of any given model. 

> Instruction prompt only mentions 'an image of' ...

We post-fix every T2I prompt with the word "realistic," e.g., “A high resolution image of Spaghetti from Italian cuisine, realistic.” These prompts can be viewed in our data release(https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CUBE_T2I_Benchmark-30C1/CUBE_1K.json). We missed adding this in Table 11 and will correct it in the camera-ready version.

> Selection of 8 countries.....and selection of USA...

Our selection of 8 countries involved several considerations which we have outlined in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG). Our initial hypothesis was that high-resource countries like **USA would serve as an upper bound for performance** (note that USA obtains highest avg faithfulness scores in Table 3), allowing meaningful comparisons with other regions. We additionally uncovered several interesting insights that even apply to countries like the USA (refer to attached PDF).
 
> Additional details on KB extraction and Refinement 

Thanks for pointing this out. We have added this detail in the general response and will update the Appendix of our  camera-ready version.

> Examples added and removed in the refinement step..

Examples discarded include erroneous KB extractions or artifacts that don't accurately represent cultural concepts. For instance, 'garlic' was removed from the 'Indian cuisine' category as it's not unique to India. The LLM extension captured missing artifacts overlooked by our KB algorithm, such as 'Warli painting' (Indian art) and 'Harumaki' (Japanese cuisine). Overall, we extended artifacts by 3-7% across countries, with <2% discarded due to noise. We will include these examples in our paper to aid understanding.

Thank you for your thorough review and for acknowledging the significance of our work. We are pleased that you view our contribution as a **fundamental step forward** and appreciate the **interdisciplinary nature** of our approach. We have responded to your comments below:

## **Clarifications**

> Maybe the authors could specify better .... how they chose specifically the 8 countries that have been chosen.


We appreciate your suggestion to clarify our selection criteria for the 8 countries. Our selection process was informed by several factors, including **rater availability** and **cost constraints**, given that we recruited raters that belonged to the specific countries we considered. Despite these considerations, we made our best efforts to ensure diverse representation across different geo-cultural regions and the Global South-North divide: Brazil (LatAm), France (Europe), India (SEA), Italy (Europe), Japan (East Asia), Nigeria (SSA), Turkey (Middle East), and the USA (North America). Given that our approach is scalable, future iterations of this work could be extended to other countries and domains. We have provided additional details on the choice of these eight countries in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG) section.

> The word "landmark" could be explained more specifically in the context of this work. As landmarks often also refer to landscapes, it creates a bit of confusion.

Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We acknowledge that the term "landmark" could cause confusion. We will clarify the distinction in our paper to ensure that the context is clear.

> Please specify why you chose H=4 in line 178

H is a hyperparameter that defines the number of hops we iterate for KB extraction. Increasing the number of hops generally results in a higher count of extracted artifacts but also leads to longer runtimes, as the number of output cache nodes for the next hop (line 8 in Algorithm 1) increases with each iteration. We observed that the majority of artifacts (i.e., WikiData nodes with country-of-origin or country property) were found within the 2nd and 3rd hops across all three domains we considered. For instance, in the art domain, with 5 hops, we extracted approximately 14%, 44%, 26%, 10%, and 6% of the total new artifacts at hops 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. A similar trend was observed in other domains, which led us to stop at 4 hops for WikiData extraction. We will include these details in the appendix of our paper.

> Are the users evaluating 1000 images? Isn't it too much? Isn't there the risk that the users get tired and the evaluation is less correct? 

No, each annotator evaluates only the images that are from the culture that they belong to. **This means each annotator rated ~120 (=1000/8) images**. Please refer to Table 7 in Appendix for a country-wise split of annotations (same as the distribution of CUBE-1K prompts).  More details on the annotations are provided in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG) as well as submitted as part of the supplementary material.

> In general, the quality of the paper would be improved if the authors added a dedicated "Limitations" section...

We thank you for pointing this out. We will add a separate limitations section in our paper following your suggestions.  

> Clarity: line 16: introduce [a] cultural diversity as a novel T2I (remove article "a") .. and typos...

Thanks for listing down several corrections that will improve the quality of our paper. We thank you for your careful review. We will make these changes in the camera-ready version.

Thank you for your thorough review and constructive feedback on our paper. We are pleased that you recognize the **critical gap we address in T2I evaluations** and appreciate the **scalability of our method to other cultures and concepts**. We have provided detailed responses to your comments below:

## **Clarifications**

> Include more countries and diverse cultural artifacts to enhance the comprehensiveness of the benchmark

Thanks for this important suggestion for extending our work. We note that this indeed aligns with our overall goal. To this end, we have designed **scalable automated pipelines for artifact extraction** that can be easily extended to more countries and cultural concepts. We will release the CUBE extraction code upon acceptance of our paper and hope that this effort will foster future work in this direction.

> How many annotators are involved in line 217?

Each image was annotated by **3 raters** who identified themselves as belonging to the respective culture. For 8 countries, we recruited a **total of 24 raters**.  We have provided more details on annotations in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG). We are happy to address any further clarifications and add it to our paper.

> I would regard this dataset as less valuable as all the images are collected by google search and manually checking procedure are not transparent to me, as described in line 200-201. Thus it's hard to identify the image quality of each cultural concept.

We assume that this comment is about the CUBE-1K dataset and its manual verification process. Please let us know if we have misunderstood. We want to clarify that we do not collect or release images as part of the CUBE benchmark. As mentioned in line 148, CUBE-CSpace is a collection of approximately 200,000 cultural artifacts, and CUBE-1K is a smaller, curated subset of prompts. These prompts are used as inputs to a T2I model to generate images. We use the number of Google Search results as a proxy for local popularity to curate the 1000 highly relevant artifacts that form the CUBE-1K prompt set (as mentioned in line 196). We have shared additional details on the self-refinement and manual checking procedures in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG)  above. Our dataset (CUBE-CSpace) is the **largest available dataset** of its kind, approximately 10 times larger than existing ones, and **CUBE-1K prompt set is a high-quality subset** for human evaluation. Please refer to Reviewer rfu1's [rebuttals](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=Y4nfSOGPQO), where we compare our automated collection efforts with other artifact collection strategies, emphasizing the scale of our method.

### **On Limitation**

> The study covers only eight countries, which may not represent the full spectrum of global cultures. and also the choice of evaluating only cuisine, landmarks, and art may be biased cultural aspects to models.

We acknowledge that the CUBE dataset currently covers 8 countries and 3 cultural concepts. We have provided additional details on the choice of these 8 countries, including the constraints, in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG) section. Additionally, we have designed scalable automated pipelines for artifact extraction that can be easily extended to more countries and cultural concepts. We will release the CUBE extraction code upon acceptance of our paper.

> The paper relies on data from WikiData and GPT-4 for refining cultural artifacts. These sources, while useful, may introduce biases and inaccuracies, affecting the quality of the benchmark.

Thank you for raising this important concern. We have acknowledged this in the Discussions section (line 367) of our manuscript. Despite this limitation, we have taken meticulous steps to mitigate potential inaccuracies, employing tools such as Google Search API, LLM self-critiquing techniques grounded in literature, and manual filtering. Moreover, as noted in line 360, this approach is only one of the many ways to expand coverage; community based approaches will bring forth complementary information. We thank you for pointing out this limitation, which we will summarize in a separate “Limitations” section in our final manuscript.

> Some sections of the paper, particularly the technical implementation of the benchmark, lack detailed descriptions, making it challenging for other researchers to replicate the study.

We have provided additional details on the technical implementation of the benchmark including KB extraction, self refinement and manual quality check in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG) section. We hope these additional details address your concerns. We will release the CUBE extraction code upon acceptance of our paper.

Thanks for taking the time to review our paper. We worry that there may be a **fundamental misunderstanding of our work**. As outlined in the general response (and highlighted by the other reviewers), the focus of our work is on evaluating models for cultural competence, and **not about studying “dataset bias and alignment”**. While our resource will enable more effective bias evaluation in generative AI, the core focus is not on dataset bias or alignment.  We have provided additional clarifications to the comments below

## **Clarifications**

> The paper does not appear to have been carefully revised..... A large number of references are not standardized....

Thank you for your comments aimed at improving the organization and readability of our paper. We will carefully revise the draft in the camera-ready version upon acceptance. 

>  The paper plans to assess large models and also uses the large models to collect data automatically, however, the amount of data is still at the level of the typical model era. 

We respectfully disagree with the above statement. CUBE-CSpace is the **largest available dataset** for generative model evaluation of culturally salient artifacts, approximately **10 times the size of the second-largest resource**. For context, we have provided a comparison of our dataset size with other similar efforts below:

| **Dataset**                    | **Artifacts Size** | **Methodology**       |
|--------------------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| DOSA ([Seth et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14651))        | **615**               | Community-Engagement  |
| CultureBank ([Shi et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15238))  | **23K**                | Automatic             |
| CAMeL ([Naous et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14456))      | **20K**                | Automatic             |
| WorldWideDishes ([Magomere et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09496)) | **765**          | Community-Engagement  |
| **CUBE-CSpace (Ours)**            | **200K**               | Automatic             |

Furthermore, our prompt dataset, CUBE-1K, consists of 1,000 prompts for T2I evaluation, which is **comparable in size to other T2I evaluation benchmarks**, such as DSG-1K (1,000 prompts), TIFA-160 (160 prompts), T2I-CompBench (6,000 prompts), PartiPrompts (1,600 prompts), and GenAI-Bench (1,600 prompts).


> They introduce manual annotation and checking to reduce data noise, but lack details of the annotation ....

We reduce data noise using two approaches: LLM-based filtering and manual quality checks. Our LLM-based filtering is well-grounded in literature, leveraging self-refinement  ([Madaan et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)) and critiquing ([Lahoti et al., 2023](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.643/)) techniques. We have provided more details of these steps in the general response ([link](https://openreview.net/forum?id=4351SumKS9&noteId=91SvLpkDTG)).

> The prompt template looks rough.

We followed standard [best practices](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/main/en/using-diffusers/weighted_prompts#prompt-engineering) for T2I prompt construction. Our prompts are templatized for ease of scalability, and such prompt templates are commonly used in T2I benchmarks (e.g., T2I-CompBench and PartiPrompts). We also utilized the best practices described in [Pavlichenko et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11711). To account for prompt variance, we averaged over five templates, as mentioned in line 715 (Appendix Section G.1). Additionally, to enhance image quality, we incorporated negative prompts, inspired by [Hao et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09611) (see Table 11 in the Appendix).



> The paper.... only evaluate two models without in-depth results analysis. It is hard to show that they solved these issues.

We would like to highlight that we evaluated **4 state-of-the-art (SOTA) T2I** models for cultural diversity. The selected models represent the best in class for *closed-source* (**Imagen**) and *open-source* (**SDXL**), as well as the top-ranked models on the [T2I-Arena Leaderboard](https://artificialanalysis.ai/text-to-image/arena) (**Playground**) and [Imsys Rankings](https://imgsys.org/rankings) (**RealVis**). Due to cost constraints in annotating model outputs with raters from specific geo-cultures, we focused on evaluating cultural awareness for 2 models: Imagen and SDXL. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has addressed cultural diversity as a T2I evaluation aspect. We believe that our effort in evaluating this aspect across 4 SOTA models, while also introducing a novel methodology, represents a significant contribution.

>  Dataset bias has long been studied, but the paper lacks investigation ....

We thank you for this suggestion. As you point out, a similar study can be performed on the training dataset. In fact, others have recently looked into such dataset biases (e.g., biases in the LAION dataset ([Birhane et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03449))). However, we would like to point out that **our focus in this paper is not dataset bias**, rather a method and resource for **evaluating model generations**.

* *Pavlichenko et al., 2022. Best Prompts for Text-to-Image Models and How to Find Them*

* *Madaan et al., 2023. Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback*
* *Lahoti et al., 2023. Improving Diversity of Demographic Representation in Large Language Models via Collective-Critiques and Self-Voting*
* *Birhane et al., 2024 "Into the laion’s den: Investigating hate in multimodal datasets." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2024)*

# General Response

**Delighted by the positive impressions of our work:**

We sincerely thank the reviewers for their time and thoughtful feedback. We are thrilled by the positive reception of our work. Reviewers found our work to be well-motivated (rfu1), a “*fundamental step forward*” (7DyQ), tackling “*an important and timely problem*” (ZPJ8), “*a critical gap*” (gYoi) and “*need of the hour*” (ZPJ8). Reviewers also found our approach to be “strongly grounded into the literature” (7DYQ), exhibiting “*a mature and needed interdisciplinary approach*” (7DYQ, and extendible to other cultural regions and concepts (gYoi). Our benchmark was also lauded as “*huge*” (ZPJ8), “*useful*” (ZPJ8, 7DYQ), and “*original*” (7DYQ). 

**Main contributions**: The focus of our paper is on evaluating cultural competence in T2I models. We develop a scalable pipeline to automatically extract cultural artifacts and use it to build a database of 200k cultural artifacts, the largest of its kind. We also introduce a novel T2I evaluation aspect: cultural diversity and discuss its importance. We believe our efforts will significantly contribute to the development of T2I models that better serve the global community.

**Points raised**: The main points raised in the reviews are 1) justification of our design choices, particularly in selecting the countries considered in this work and 2) lack of technical details for benchmark dataset construction. We have addressed these details below and responded to specific reviewer queries in our rebuttals. We look forward to an engaging discussion.

## Justification for the choice of countries 

We selected eight countries from different geo-cultural regions across continents and the Global South-North divide: Brazil (LatAm), France (Europe), India (SEA), Italy (Europe), Japan (East Asia), Nigeria (SSA), Turkey (Middle East), and USA (North America). Our goal was to choose countries with the largest population in each of these regions, while also taking into account (a) their representation in training data (e.g. Nigeria is “low-resource” whereas USA is “high-resource”), and (b) availability of raters from that region through our vendor. We limited our study to 8 countries because of time and monetary constraints. While we acknowledge that this list of countries is necessarily incomplete, and may result in a biased global sampling, future iterations of this work could include a wider range of countries for a more comprehensive evaluation.

## Technical Details for CUBE construction

Below we have added additional details on our benchmark construction process. We will add this to the appendix of our paper.

**KB Extraction**

We have reported the root nodes for each domain in Table 6 in Appendix. Further, we iterated for a total of 4 hops beginning from these root nodes. This is because we found that the majority of the artifacts were found in the second and third hop for all the 3 domains we considered. The new artifacts extracted began to plateau after the 4th hop. We will release the CUBE Wikidata extraction code upon acceptance of our paper to foster extension of our work to other domains/countries.

**Self refinement**

We divide the self refinement of the concept space into two steps:
* Removing noise: An incorrect artifact that does not belong to either that country or cultural concept. We leverage LLMs for this filtering step by asking “Can you classify if the <item> belongs to <country> <concept>? Answer yes or no.”
* Adding missing artifacts: We leverage the self-critiquing technique introduced in [Lahoti et al.,](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.643/) 2023 by following “critique the response” and “address the critiques and rewrite” steps for each of the artifact lists. 

We will add the prompts used for these steps in the Appendix in the camera-ready version.

**Manual Filtering**

CUBE-1K is intended to serve as a high-quality curated prompt set to represent cultural artifacts selected for *relevance* and *popularity*. As noted in line 197, we use the *local* Google Search results as a proxy for popularity within that local context. While this provides us with a broad set of artifacts in each cultural context, some of them may show inflated results because of the commonality of certain words in their names (e.g., “Puri” is the name of a famous temple in India and also a popular dish.). To mitigate this, we used a manual filtering process conducted by annotators from their respective cultures. This process removes any artifacts that may have been artificially boosted by inflated search results. *The criteria for manual filtering include visual distinctiveness, alignment with the corresponding geo-cultural category, and the artifact's popularity within the culture*. 


**Annotator details for CUBE**

Our annotators were recruited based on the following criteria: 
* Be fluent in English 
* Be diverse in Gender
* Be from specific countries with familiarity of local culture

We considered 8 countries and recruited 3 raters from each country - a total of 24 raters.
Each rater annotated all the images from their respective country (~120-130 images per rater) as per the rater guidelines detailed in the Appendix. See Table 7 in Appendix for country-wise distribution of annotation in CUBE-1K. Each image, thus received a 3-way annotation from the 3 raters considered. 

We have submitted a pdf titled ‘additional_human_annotation_details.pdf’  as well as a datacard for our benchmark in the supplementary material.

summary_and_contributions.value:
Paper has three contributions: 
1. Paper provides a dataset of cultural artifacts from 8 countries and 3 concepts, to pave the way for cultural awareness and cultural diversity analysis of text-to-image models. 
2. Provides a benchmark dataset over 1000 prompts where model-generated images are evaluated by human raters (with relevant geographical expertise) for faithfulness and realism.
3. Introduces a diversity score based on existing literature with modifications, to evaluate the cultural diversity of model-based generations for open-ended prompts.

review.value: Please find my review in the questions that follow.

strengths.value:
The paper is tackling an important and timely problem, in a time where models are being deployed across cultures but continue to exhibit biases in representation. Further, in relation to related work, the paper goes beyond what exists in the literature and takes on novel problems in this space which is commendable. 

The dataset CUBE-CSpace is huge and stands to be a useful resource in future research on culture-based analysis of generative models. Further, if the code for generation is made available, with ease of reproducibility, I believe this is a good contribution. 

The paper provided end-to-end methodology for evaluating cultural diversity in a mostly automated fashion, enable efficient large-scale analysis, which is an important need of the hour.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Question for authors: 

-- Since the methodology for generating CUBE-CSpace is automated, why was the choice made to limit this to 8 countries? 
To allow this methodology to be used for other countries, concepts, would the code for generating a similar dataset be shared on the Internet?

-- It would be interesting the run the cultural diversity metric on existing datasets (be it prompt sets or prompt-image sets) to compare the outcomes of the CD metric against other metrics used in T2I evaluation. This will also enable understanding on how CD does or does not complement other evaluation metrics.

limitations.value:
The paper could be improved by providing more fine-grained details of the methodology employed in this work. This will help the reader understand and contextualise the results in the paper, and also support reproducibility and reusability, which are key features of datasets and benchmarks. 

> Criteria for cultural awareness
- The paper studies cultural awareness over largely two dimensions: (1) faithfulness and (2) realism. It is not made clear in the paper why is realism a salient factor for evaluating cultural awareness. For instance, what if the model tends to make more animated/non-realistic images of food independent of the cultural context. Is that necessarily a bad thing? 
- Further, the instruction prompt only mentions 'an image of' which can be understood to mean any type of image, is that not correct?

> We select eight countries from different geo-cultural regions across continents and the Global South-North divide: Brazil, France, India, Italy, Japan, Nigeria, Turkey, and USA
- How was this selection done? Why choose USA when it is one of the most well-represented countries in existing models?


> Regarding section 3
- Please provide more details about KB Extraction and Refinement in the Appendix for guiding readers and supporting reusability and reproducibility. 
- It is not clear from the outset what types of examples would have been thrown out in the refinement step and added in the refinement step. Please provide examples with explanations to support understanding of the methodology. 

> Therefore, the final collection undergoes a manual verification process to ensure the quality and relevance of selected artifacts. Table 7 presents the distribution of artifacts across different countries.
 - What does the manual verification process consider as criteria for filtering? 
 - What types of noisy outcomes were observed after the first pass of the query-popularity method?

> Line 203 We specifically provide a negative prompt to obtain images of cultural artifacts with desirable qualities.
- Negative prompt has not been introduced yet, and it is hard to guess the definition given the context.  
- Where does the negative prompt get used in the cultural-awareness analysis?

> On page 5, under human annotation: 
- It is important to inform the reader how many annotations were done by each human participant and how many annotations were received by each prompt-image pair, to understand the size of the data
- It is very interesting to see disagreement among participants from the same geographical regions on image faithfulness, and a further exploration of that in that paper would have been very interesting to see. This would support understanding of the subjectivity of such evaluations and the reasons behind it. 

> In sec 5.2 on experimental setup
- How to ensure that every correctly generated image finds a mapping in the CUBE artifact collection. For instance: it is possible to have images whose related terms are not present in the CUBE dataset. 
- How to check for errors in the mapping function: It is possible that the image is incorrect and does not map to anything, however the mapping function maps it to something in the dataset.

title.value: Very nice work with some things to be fixed

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors propose a framework to evaluate the cultural competence of T2I models considering cultural awareness and cultural diversity (that they define in their work). With the existing body of work on biases in generative models, such a contribution represents a fundamental step forward in understanding the behavior of this models and providing context for practitioners and researchers to develop a more critical understanding of them.

review.value:
- timely contribution that goes beyond the mere evaluation of biases without culturally contextualizing the images generated by these models
- the justification and motivation of the work are particularly clear and grounded on research and understanding from different academic fields
- the benchmark is original and useful
- the approach using KB is strongly grounded into the literature and particularly appreciated in this context

strengths.value:
- In a landscape of research that focuses on AI ethics almost as it was a mere checklist, I cannot do anything but appreciate the efforts of the authors to provide a more nuanced perspective on the topic of biases in T2I generation, considering cultural artifacts and expressions. 
- The justification of each choice is grounded in literature that goes beyond the field of computer science, showing a mature and needed interdisciplinary approach to the subject matter.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- Maybe the authors could specify better why they were limited in the choice of the countries and how they chose specifically the 8 countries that have been chosen. 
- The word "landmark" could be explained more specifically in the context of this work. As landmarks often also refer to landscapes, it creates a bit of confusion.
- Please specify why you chose H=4 in line 178

limitations.value:
- Are the users evaluating 1000 images? Isn't it too much? Isn't there the risk that the users get tired and the evaluation is less correct? Maybe some considerations about this would be helpful.
- In general, the quality of the paper would be improved if the authors added a dedicated "Limitations" section, so that other authors would be aware of all the limitations of this work.

correctness.value: The claims and the results are mostly correct.

clarity.value:
- line 16: introduce [a] cultural diversity as a novel T2I (remove article "a")
- line 152 you refer to table 7 which is in the supplementary material. I am not sure that this is the right way to use supplementary material (referecing it in the main text). In any case, I would specify that it's in the appendix and not in the main text when you refer to it in line 152.
- line 205: cultural awareness of ... and then the sentence is cut by a comma
- line 695 has a broken reference...

relation_to_prior_work.value: The Related Work section is concice and clear and it helps contextualizing the work better. Table 1 is particularly helpful in understanding how this paper positions compared to existing efforts.

documentation.value: The documentation is clear. The readme could include more instructions for the users and reproducing the experiments, rather than just an indexed summary of the material included in the repository.

additional_feedback.value: In the related work section you say that IS and FID were used for early T2I evaluation. I would specify that these metrics were not initially thought for T2I models, as they are a derivation of what was used on other visual generative models (e.g., GANs).

title.value: Beyond Aesthetics: Cultural Competence in Text-to-Image Models

TLDR.value: A new cultural competence benchmark for T2I with cultural diversity as a novel metric for T2I evaluation.

abstract.value: Text-to-Image (T2I) models are being increasingly adopted in diverse global communities where they create visual representations of their unique cultures. Current T2I benchmarks primarily focus on faithfulness, aesthetics, and realism of generated images, overlooking the critical dimension of *cultural competence*. In this work, we introduce a framework to evaluate cultural competence of T2I models along two crucial dimensions: cultural awareness and cultural diversity, and present a scalable approach using a combination of structured knowledge bases and large language models to build a large dataset of cultural artifacts to enable this evaluation. In particular, we apply this approach to build CUBE (CUltural BEnchmark for Text-to-Image models), a first-of-its-kind benchmark to evaluate cultural competence of T2I models. CUBE covers cultural artifacts associated with 8 countries across different geo-cultural regions and along 3 concepts: cuisine, landmarks, and art. CUBE consists of 1) CUBE-1K, a set of high-quality prompts that enable the evaluation of cultural awareness, and 2) CUBE-CSpace, a larger dataset of cultural artifacts that serves as grounding to evaluate cultural diversity. We also introduce cultural diversity as a novel T2I evaluation component, leveraging quality-weighted Vendi score. Our evaluations reveal significant gaps in the cultural awareness of existing models across countries and provide valuable insights into the cultural diversity of T2I outputs for underspecified prompts. Our methodology is extendable to other cultural regions and concepts and can facilitate the development of T2I models that better cater to the global population.

def process(client, invitation):

    venue_id = domain.id

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
